prompt: A reliable bulk-transfer link has a high raw rate, long feedback delay and residual losses after coding. Which design choices merit consideration? Select all that apply.

options.text: Use suitable FEC to reduce residual errors without a retransmission round trip
options.explanation: Correct. Coding trades redundancy and decoding work for repair; its effectiveness depends on the code and channel.

options.text: Allow a pipeline rather than waiting for each individual frame's ACK
options.explanation: Correct. A long feedback interval can leave stop-and-wait mostly idle when frame transmission is short.

options.text: Consider selective recovery that retains later correctly received frames after a gap
options.explanation: Correct. It can avoid Go-Back-N's repeated work, at the cost of memory and bookkeeping.

options.text: Always choose the largest possible frame, regardless of error behaviour
options.explanation: Larger frames reduce relative header overhead but expose more bits to damage under independent errors; the best size depends on coding and recovery.

options.text: Minimise the sequence-number field regardless of the required window
options.explanation: Sequence space must support unambiguous window operation and safe reuse; reducing header size cannot override correctness.

workedExample: Consider three resources: airtime, feedback time and receiver state. FEC can spend extra bits and processing to repair some damage locally. Pipelining covers the long feedback interval with outstanding work. Selective recovery retains later successes instead of resending everything after a gap. Balance these gains against coding overhead, buffering and safe sequence-number reuse; raw bit-error probability alone does not establish residual frame loss.
